parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a fleet technician. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
To start, could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start your shift until you leave?

I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. During my day, I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send drones to charge.
How do you find out which drones need repairs or charging when you start your shift?
I don't know.
Who hands work over to you during the day, and who do you hand work off to?
I don't know.
Could you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
What are the things you currently check by hand because you don't trust the existing numbers or systems?
I don't know.
Right after something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what is the first thing you need to know?
I don't know.
When you think about a new service being built for your work, what are you most afraid it might do wrong?
I don't know.
When you add a new drone to the fleet, what information do you need to record about it?
I don't know.
Could you tell me more about what happens when you take a drone out of service for repairs and later put it back?
I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back in working order. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
What do the regulators ask to see when they want to know how your drones have been looked after?
I don't know.
When you set up charging pads at your sites or send drones to charge, what does that process look like for you?
I set up charging pads at our sites, and each of us has a few dozen of them. I also send drones to charge, using our charging equipment.
How do you decide which charging pad to send a drone to?
I don't know.
What happens when you retire an old drone from the fleet?
I retire old drones from the fleet as part of keeping our equipment in working order. I don't know what happens after that.
Is there anything else about your work with the drones, charging pads, or regulators that you can tell me?

I keep the drones and charging equipment in working order by adding new drones, retiring old ones, and sending them to charge. I also set up charging pads at our sites, and take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
